note.value: SIR RICHARD HADDOCK TO PHILIP FROWD.

text.p: Tower Hill, London, this 29th July, 1688. Sr,

The last week, in a news lettr wrote by a served of yours, one Mr. Edmd Sawkell, there is a scandalous reflection on my honr and reputation, by his writing that Sr Rd Haddock with several other seamen were gone into Holland, which I have recd acct of sd letter from 3 or 4 counties, and must believe it hath flown all the kingdom over.

Sr, I was this day to waite on you at ire post ofice; but, having acct given me that you were in the country, thought fit, before I spake with Mr. Sawkill, to give you notice hereof, and yt you will readily conclude I shall expect satisfaction from him for this scandal, at least yt he finds out his author or else must conclude him to be the inventor himself. I do presume you know me so well as to believe, however the King may please to deal with me (which hitherto hath bine extra kind), I shall never forsake my loyalty and duty to him, even to my last breath. Praying a lyne or two in answer, with great respect, I remain
Your very afecte servant,
Rd H.
To In. Frowd, Esq.

note.value: CAPTAIN JOSEPH HADDOCK TO HIS BROTHER, SIR RICHARD HADDOCK.

text.p: Aboard the Ship Princess of Denmark, 17th Xber, 1688. Balasore Road.
Sr Richd Haddock.
My ever hond Brother,

My last, of the 7th Augt from Visagapatam, gave your Honr acct of our arrival Madras and of our affairs to that time. The 10th Augt we sailed thence for Balasore, where we arrived the 15th; in which bay we have contd and rid out the monsoon, which has proved favourabler then expected (being leap year).

The 15th 7ber Capt Heath arrived this place, who, by virtue of the President and Counsel of Madras order required my going up with him to Chuttynutte in the river of Hugly (the place where our Agent and factory resided), myself with the rest of the comandrs of the Europe Ships then in the river to assist him in the Rt Honble Comps affairs. In fews days after our getting up to Chuttynutte, a letter was writ to the Nabob of Dacca (the chief govenr of that city), who had formerly requested our Agent that if we would assist him with ships to transport solders and horse from Chottagam to Arraccan (they being in wars with that King), he would give us his Pharwanna of a settlemt of trade, with privileges as formerly according to the 12 articles formerly sent him from our agent &c. Capt. Heath, in the letter sent, condescended to
the Nabob's request, in supplying him with 10 ships and vessels for the Mogul's occations, to transport there solders and horse, provided they would allow of the building of a fortyfiction wthin the river of Hugly, for the better security of the Rt Honble Comps estate and serts; without which grant of a fortified place the Comps ordrs positive are, to wthdraw off all our factory from this place.

We continued here 5 weeks for the Nabob's answer to the proposal: but not coming, we, having taken off all the Honble Comps concerns from the shore, sailed from Chuttynty the 8th 9ber, and passed by there forts peaceably. At our arrival Balasore found that the govenr of the town had (some time before our coming) detained the Rt Honble Comps goods, being this years investmts, also parts. men's goods; and would not permit none of the factors, nor our people that were ashore buying provisions , to come off. Capt Heath sent 2 of our factors with a letter to the govenr (who was come down to the bancksall, or point of sand going into the river, where he was making a fortification), to demand the Rt Honbe Comps goods with all our men. His answer was, what he did was by order from the Nabob; and, if he did deliver our goods and men, should loose his head. 3 days after, 2 of the factors were again sent to acquaint the govenr that our intention was to depart out these parts peaceable, we having come away out Hugly river without doeinge any act of hostility to any of the Mogul's subjects; therefore required him to send off our goods and people by fair means; if not, we would have them by force of arms. Which hee not permitting them too go off, the next day all our solders, about 320, and upwards 240 seamen were put into the small vessels and all our boats; and early next morning they landed a mile to the W.ward of the fort (which the govnr had raised); against which landing place they had planted 5 small guns on a sandhill, which they discharged at our men, and killed 2 and wounded 2 more; so fled from the guns. And soon after, the chief capt of our solders had drawn all the solders and seamen in order of battalion, marched up to the fort, which, at there approach, fired all there guns they had
planted to the land; but, soon after, the govenr and all his men fleed out the fort without doing much harm to our men; the which we possessed without any farther opposition. In and about this fort they had upwards 40 guns mounted and a good wall made with timber and clay; might have bine sufficient (if managed by Europeans) to have wthstood a great army of men, or at least done much more mischief then they did.

The govenr, after deserted his fort, made all hast possible up to Balasore town, and ordered the factory house (in which were confined all our people, thirteen in number) to be set on fire. Our people in the house defended themselves bravely, killing sevl of the Moors; but by the firsness of the fire were forced to surrender themselves on terms to have there lives and good usage. The next day Capt. Heath (who went ashore with the solders - Capt Sharpe commanded the small vessels and boats that were to go over the barr, leaving me in command of the ships in the road) went up with all the solders and seamen to Balasore town by watter and landed short of old Balasore fort, the which they soon took; so marched into the town, few or no people being left to oppose them; the govenr deserting it at there coming, carrying with him all our English, amongst which are 3 of our ships comp, vizt. Mr. Davenant (being ashore buying provisions ), Charles Scarlet, midshipman, and Sam Harbin, gunr, sert of Capn Heath's, his pursur, and 3 more, Mr. Stanly, chief of the factory, the rest free men that trades in the country. As yet we cannot get the govenr to give there releasemt. We have sent sevl messengers to him, that we have not burnt there town nor ships, expecting he would deliver up our men; but, if not, we will return and doe both. Our solders (but seamen more espetially) have committed many inhuemane actions in the town, plundering not only Moors but sevl Portugeese houses, and killed sevl innocent people. We have had the greatest loss in this axtion, vizt. 4 men killed and 3 wounded. There names are: Mr. Starland, 3d mate, Henry Grove, chief trumpeter, Christopher Hog, and Jno Hinton, who very indiscreetly
went out with sevl more seamen to a garden house, expecting great plunder, were cut off, sevl of them, by a party of horse. The 3 wounded are Henry Roxby, Frans Johnson, and Jno Smart.

I have, by the Williamson (by whom this is also intended you), sent Sr Henry Johnson and Sr Tho. Rawlinson, and also to my wife, a list of our dead &ca men, in all 44. Our supernumery men which I brought out of England, being 27, at my arrival Madras, I aquaintd the President therwth, who offred them to Cap. Bromwell, the Rotchester having lost most of there men. But he refusing to pay the charge the Honble Comp were at sending them out, they were not taken out there; and what of them that are alive doe still remain in our ship, not being demanded here by the agent. I suppose our owners will be allowed for them at 50s per mo, no longer then our departure Madras, to which time we had lost 30 men. I doe not repent there continueinge aboard, having had so great mortolaty and most of them the best of our seamen.

I suppose our next enterprise will be towards Chottagam, a place near the coast of Arraccan. The Rt Honble Comp positive orders are for endeavouring the taking it; but I fear we shall not have strength sufficient to effect it, the Nabob having sent many thousand of men this year there to over run and take the kingdom of Arracan. The king of that country being some time since dead, part of the people are in rebelion against the present govermt; by which its supposed the Mogullers will go far in taking that country this year, and we frustrated of our design.

Honble Sir, I have not wrote to any of owners (except the 2 in charty party), believing we shall return to Madras before the Williamson sails for England. Our ship is in a very good condition and very thite. I believe our stay in India will be the extreme of our time, for at present no prospect of a freight for Europe; and I fear the brave trade of Bengal will be lost, at which the Dutch and French rejoice, that this trade may wholly fall to them.

I have not else to add; only please to present my duty, respects,
and love to all our dear relations and friends. Thus, with my due respects to your self and my good lady sister, doe remain,
Honble Sr, your affectionate bro. and Sert, whilst
Jose Haddock.
Sr I recd your letter, also one from my wife sent per the Defence; and return my humble thancks for it.
For the Honble Sr Richd Haddock, at his house on Tower Hill. Present. London.
Pr the Williamson, Capt. Ashby, Comandr, D. G.

note.value: RICHARD HADDOCK TO HIS FATHER, SIR RICHARD HADDOCK.

text.p: April ye 23d 1692 ; Monday, in ye Hook. Honoured Sr,

This is to acquaint of our engaging with ye French and of our having got ye victory. Wee met ym of sea, May 19. There was about 60 sail. Wee fought ym from 11 to 9 att night; since which, have been in pursuit of ym. There is run ashore, in Sherbrook bay, Torveil with 3 more capital ships, which are now burned. Cozen Tom Heath burnt Torveil; and have chased 14 sail more in ye Hook, where wee now are. Sr Cloudsly Shovel is going in with ye 3d rates and fire-ships to destroy ym. Wee have been so unfortunate
as to lose Rear Admll Carter in ye fight. I am very well and have received no wound; only a small splinter hit me on ye thigh, but did no damage, only made it black and blew. I would write more particularly, but ye vessel I hear is going away presently; so, having no more att present, butt duty to your self and my mother,
I remain your dutiful Son,
Richd Haddock.
Cozen Ruffin is alive and very well. I will write ye particulars of our fight as soon as wee come into any port.
Rd H.
For Sr Richd Haddock, att ye Navy Office, in Crutched Fryers, London.

note.value: SIR RICHARD HADDOCK TO HIS SON RICHARD.

text.p: Navy Office, this 27th Novr, 1702.
Dear Son,

I have yors of yesterday's date, from the Downs, which brings us the joyful tydeings of your safe arrival there. Your long passage from Newfoundland put us in great fear of your welfare, and particularly your more hath bine for a month or 5 weeks crying for you and your brother Nics safety; but blessed be God you are both come well home. Your bror now with us came up from the Downs by leave from his Captn, and hath behaved himself with so much bravery and couradge that he hath gained the good report of the Duke of Ormond, his Captn, &c., both in the action at Rotta and St. Mary Port, and Vigo, and was the first man that borded one of the galleons at Vigo, which is come home. I do not find by your letter that you were with your Comodore at the taking and destroying the French ships to the southwards of Trepassa, and consequently you will not come in for your share of that capture. The news papers tells us your prize is got into Plymo, and for your boat with 5 men you say you left behind at Plymo we never heard anything of it, which gives you trouble; and because you write not of my Cos Wm's welfare, I am conscernd for fear he might be in that boat. To morrow morning I intend to go to ye Admty and endeavour you may come into the River, if his R. Highness orders your cleaneing.

God Almighty hath blessed ye forces of her Majty and her Allies,
both by land and sea, in a wonderful manner; for which we lately had a public day of thanksgiveing in this city. The Queen, House of Lords and Commons, with the Bishops, Judges, &c. came to St Pal's Church, where, after sermon, Te Deum was sung.

Since your leaving England, two of our board are dead, vizt. Mr. Sotherne and my good friend Comr Willshaw, who dyed ye 23d Sepr last. My Cos Anna Babb, that was in one of our alms houses at Stepny, is likewise dead, and my poor Cozn Lockwood's son in law, Cozn Hodges, dyed lately at Gosport, since his arrival from Codex and Vigo, who waited a tender on ye Duke of Ormond's ship. We are all in good health, praised be God, and do kindly salut you. I am your most afectiont father,
Rd Haddock.

Pray let me know how your ship proves. I have concerned my self to get one of ye 4th rates building at Deptford for you, and this day spake to Sr Goo. Rooke about it, and formerly to ye other 3 Council of ye Lord High Admll. I know she is tender by your reifeing your courses; and it was well hinted in yours to ye Admty. I am glad you past by Plymo. Orders went thither some time since to clean you and several of your consarts.
Rd H.
On Her Majesty's Service. To Captn Richard Haddock, Comandr of her Majty Ship the Reserve, these present, In ye Downs.

note.value: SIR RICHARD HADDOCK TO HIS SON RICHARD HADDOCK

text.p: Navy Office, this 10th Decembr, 1703. My dear Son,

Your letter of the 17th Novr past, giving me acct of the unhappy disaster of your ship being run ashore by a Dutch pilot and of your happy getting off again, I recd 3 or 4 ds. after its date; but, hoping
you might have got away before an answer could arrive you, I forbore answering it to you to Helvoet Sluice. I have just now recd yours of the 7th instant, Tuesday, and, to our great joy, the acct of God Almighty's wonderful preservation of you in the late most dreadful storm, which no man living can remember the like. I perceive you have had an acct of the most sad and lamentable efects of it here in England, not only in the loss of our shipping , but about 1500 men in the Queen's ships. I shall not eneumerate ye particulars of the loss, only that Capt. Emes, with his wife and son and all ye men in ye Restoration, lost on ye Goodwin, and poor Tom Blake drowned at Bristol in ye Canterbury store ship cast away. The Dorcetshire we have acct of her being on ye back of Yarmo Sands, cruseing, I suppose for want of anchors and cables, and hope ye Association is cruseing in the sea on the like occasion. My dear son Nico happened to be sick on board her, as Sr S. Fairebone wrote me from the Downs. I sent Tom Apleby immediately to Deal to bring him up; but the ship sailed ye morning before he got down. I hope he will come well home to us. Pray God the Russell may be got of ye sands and into Helvoet Sluice.

Wee have 7 or 8 vessels with anchors and cables in Harwch or Oasely bay, ready to put to sea when we hear where Sr Stafford is. Sr Cloud. Shovel I hope now safe at the Nor; his mainemast cut down after he had drove 3 legs from ye Longsd, very near the Galloper. Ye St Goo. and R. Oak, now at Blackstakes, rode out ye storm without damage; and the Cambridge I believe the same. The 4 ships that broke from their ground takle was the Association, Russell, Revenge, and Dorcetshire. The Revenge was in Solebay some time since, and furnish with anchors and cables from ye Nottingham and another man of war yt went out Yarmo roads to look for our ships. Capt. Kerr in ye Revenge gave acct that he saw
ye Association, Monday last was seven-night; so that we are in hope she is very well. I shall not enlarge, only to give you our kind saluts. Pray God send you with ye King of Spain well out that place and over to us. My hearty and humble service to Sr Goo: Rooke.
I am your most afect father,
R.H.

note.value: NICHOLAS HADDOCK TO HIS FATHER SIR RICHARD HADDOCK.

text.p: St George in Barcelona Road, this 1st of May, 1706, O.S. Hond Sr,

This comes to you by the Falcon pink, which is sent home express with the good news of our reliving Barcelona in the greatest extremity. The French had made preparations for a general assault that very day we came; and it must have been infallibly taken, had we not had the luckiest passage imaginable (being but five days from Lisbon to Cape Martin, where we joined Sr Jno. Leake).

Saturday last in the morning, when were about 5 leagues to the wtward of Barcelona, my Lord Peterborow came of to the fleet with twleve hundd soldiers embarked in felucas and boats, and in the afternoon got in and landed them, with all the soldiers out of the transports and most of the marines of the fleet. We have now about nine thousand soldiers in the town. The French army consisted at first of twenty thousand; four of which, horse under the command of the Duke of Anjou. Their loss during this siege is computed to be five thousand including a thousand sick and wounded they have left behind, when they raised the siege, which was at twelve o'clock last night. They have left 50 pieces of brass cannon mounted and 15 mortars, and are now bound to Roussilion. They will find great difficulties on their march. The Miquelets, being very numerous and all in arms, will destroy a great many of 'em before they get out of Catalonia, it being a close country. The French squadron before this place consisted of 26 sail, line of battle ships. They sailed the night before we came, having intelligence of us by their scouts. They were all the supply the army had for provisions, for the Catalans have not given them the least; nor could a man of 'em stir from his tent a musket shot out of the Camp but they killed him. We are now sending four ships with
6 hundred soldiers for Girone, to reinforce that garrison, lest the French should make any attempt on it, it lying in their way.

I hear there is an express come to Barcelona from my Lord Gallaway, giving an account of his being got to Toledo and on his march for Madrid. The lucky turn Providence has given to our affairs in these parts I suppose will be joyful news in England; and this being the first certain acct you'll have, this long letter wont seem tedious.

I can expect no letters from you till Sr Clowdsly join us, and then do hope shall hear of your welfare and some good news in return of all this, which, with my duty to ire self and mother and love to all friends, is from,
Hond Sir, Ire dutiful Son,
Ns Haddock.

P.S. We have had an eclipse of the sun to-day; lasted above two hours, and for a quarter it was total and as dark as night. With it may portend, I leave to the learned. Our fleet consists of 50 sail in the line; 13 of which, Dutch.

note.value: NICHOLAS HADDOCK TO HIS FATHER SIR RICHARD HADDOCK.

text.p: Alicant, this 31st of July, 1706.
Hond Sr,

I have both ire letters by Captn Delevall, as also the butter and cheeses, for which I return you thanks. I'm glad to hear both my sisters are so well recovered by the Bath. Pray God continue their healths. Sunday last we took this place, attacking it by land and sea; and almost all the people of it are run up to the castle, with the garrison, for protection. We assisted our army with 500 seamen. I have been ashore with 50 of our ship's company during
the siege; am very heartily fateigued, but very well in health. After we have got the castle, I hear the fleet will go for the Islands of Minorca and Majorca, and, after that, I hope home. If the St George should not do, intend asking Sr Jno Leake leave for my self.

I'm glad to hear the ship at Sheernes will be launched so soon as March. I hope I'm pretty secure of her. I desire your excuse for this bad scrawle and blotted paper, but I write with a pen made with an old razor that I find in the house I'm quartered in. I have no more to say but my duty to ire self and mother and love to all friends in London and Mile end, and remain,
Hond Sr, Ire dutiful Son,
N. Haddock.
P.S. This lettr goes by the Rye.
To Sr Richd Haddock, at the Navy Office in Crutched Friars, London, these.

note.value: SIR RICHARD HADDOCK TO THE COMMISSIONERS OF THE ADMIRALTY.

text.p: 25th July, 1709.
Gentlemen,

In the year 1672 I commanded as Captn of the Royal James, under the Rt Honble the Earl of Sandwch, in the Soul Bay fight. The said ship, after a vigorous defence, was burnt by the Dutch; in which action I was wounded, the cure of which cost me, in surgeons, apothecary, nurses, &c., betwixt four score and a hundred pounds. I have bine so remiss and negligent as not to demand satisfaction for my reimbursemt. Do pray the favour of the board I may have a bill made out, what you shall think convenient, having bine out of my money now 36 is. I likewise, in the year 1690 (being then one of the Comrs for Victualling), was taken into custody at Portsmo,
and brought up a prisoner from thence by order of the then House of Commons, and remained as such a considerable time in ye hands of Mr. Topham, then sergant at arms to sd house, under pretence of our poisoning the fleet then at sea (under combed of Admll Herbert, now Earl of Torrington), with guts in our beer and gaules in our beef; and with great dificulty obtained to be bailed. I must not call it injustice in that august assembly, what they did to me; but it cost me about a hundred pounds to Mr. Topham for his fees, and to lawyers soliciting the House of Commons, with expenses of entertainment whilst in custody; for satisfaction of which I presume the board will not think fit to allow me, except directed so to doe by order of the Lord High Admll, for which shall make my application to him; but for my cure, I doubt not the favour and justice of the board in ordering a bill to be made out.
I remain, Gentn, your very humble served,
Rd. Haddock.

note.value: SIR RICHARD HADDOCK TO HIS GRANDSON.

text.p: Clapham, 28th May, 1712, Wedensday.
Dear Grandson,
I came yesterday to this place, and, according to my promise, do answer yours of 18th instant from Christ College in Oxford.

It happens to be this day 40 years that I was burnt out of the Royal James in the Sole Bay fight against the Dutch. Am well pleased to find the efforts you intend to make yourself famous in Westminster Hall. It is like the saying of your Uncle Nichs, who doubted not but to be as great as Sr Cloudesly Shovel was; and he pushes very fair for it. Your father and family went to Wakehurst
Satuarday last; took Betty and Fanny Clark down with them; got well thither. Your Uncle Richard, the week past, hath bine very ill with a feavor and ague, which kept me from hence longer then I designed; is under the advice of Doctor Ratclif, who gave me leave to come down hither, promiseing his care of him; and was down stairs when came away.
With my hearty prayers for your health and welfare, I am
Your most afect grandfather,
Rd. H.

note.value: CAPTAIN NICHOLAS HADDOCK TO HIS WIFE.

text.p: Grafton at sea, about 10 leagues from Cape Passaro, Aug. the 4th, 1718.
My dr Fanny,
The Superb being ordered from the fleet with the Admiral's letters, I send this to tell you I am well.

Five days ago we had a battle with the Spanish fleet off of Cape Passaro, on the Island of Sicily, in which several of their ships were taken and some destroyed. The Grafton had her share in that action, and the Admiral has been pleased to make me great compliments on my behaviour that day. I shall soon be ordered to be refitted at Port Mahon, the ship requiring it. I had fifty men killed and wounded. Among the former was Lt Bramble, who was appointed by the interest of Sir Cha. Wager. I'm sorry for him, he being a
good officer. My Cousin Haddock chased towards the shore after part of the Spanish fleet, when they separated, with 4 or 5 other ships whose signals were made for that purpose, and they are not yet come into the fleet. However, I doubt not but he is well, the ships that they were sent after being of the smaller sort.
My dr, pray send to Mrs. Harris to tell her her spouse is well. He dined aboard me the day after the action; he was one of the ships engaged.
Just before we sailed from Naples I received ire letter, and am glad to hear yrself and the little boy are well. I give my love to all friends, and remain, my dr Fanny,
Ire most affect husband,
Ns. Haddock.

note.value: CAPTAIN NICHOLAS HADDOCK TO HIS WIFE.

text.p: Grafton, at Regio, Janry the 19th, O.S., 1718/9. My dear Spouse,

I send this to tell you I am well. I believe, before this come to you, you will have heard of my having forced ashore on Sicily a Spanish man of war of 70 guns, which is overset and sunk. I recd some shot from her, but without much damage. My dr, we are here at an anchor, in company with the Kent, Roil Oak, and Rochester, to block up Camock, who is at Messina and will not venture out,
his squadron being much inferior to us. By the news we receive from England, I conjecture Spain will soon be oblidgd to accept the terms proposed to 'em; after which I suppose the bigger ships will be ordered home, where I shall always be glad to be, whenever it consists with my honour; for, indeed, my dear Fanny, I heartily love you.
Pray give my love to all friends, and I remain, my dr,
Ire most affect. husband,
Ns. Haddock.
P.S. This goes for Naples with an express that Capt. Matthews sends to the Adml, and from thence it will be forwarded to you.
Ns H.
